fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Two Birth Stories, Told Straight Through", "body": "Both hosts open with newborn daughters barely a week old. Jorge Mesa describes an unplanned bathtub delivery after the doulas and midwife all arrived too late, an hour and twenty five minutes of active labor, a forty inch umbilical cord, and the moment he got his own hands underneath and caught the baby. Chance Garton counters with a birth center seven minutes from his house, a shower, a pool, his wife saying she knew what she had to do but was scared, and a giant tuning fork struck once before the final contraction delivered a baby still in an intact bag of waters."}, {"title": "Naming a Child by the Numbers", "body": "Gracie Gabriella Garton and Indigo Autumn Lark Mesa get run through the septenary cipher live on screen. Chance explains that Gracie sums to twenty six, the same value he assigns the Yod Heh Vav Heh, that Gabriella with one L pushes the initials to triple seven, and that Ella and Grace are both great grandmothers on the family tree. Jorge says Petra maintains the baby told her the name rather than the parents choosing it. Slick Dissident adds that grace is the remedial virtue of the enneagram number two, which he calls the giver, his own type."}, {"title": "Alvin Boyd Kuhn on the Festival of Lost Meanings", "body": "The spine of the show is a short 1922 pamphlet by Alvin Boyd Kuhn, which Jorge pulled off the newly restored Internet Archive. Kuhn's argument, as the three read it aloud, is that Halloween is one of four cardinal festivals keyed to the equinoxes and solstices, that the zodiac maps the soul's descent through sensation, emotion, mind and spirit, and that Halloween falls forty days after the September equinox because forty marks the whole span of soul entering matter. Chance reframes the fall not as original sin but as incarnation, from the Latin for flesh."}, {"title": "The Doctrine of Necessity and Inverted Occam's Razor", "body": "Slick Dissident builds a long weave: the doctrine of necessity abbreviates to DON, FEMA is named for a goddess who multiplies rumor and information, and multiplying necessity by rumor produces the exact opposite of Occam's razor, whose Latin form warns against multiplying entities. Chance translates it as the truth movement generating endless conjecture with few kernels of truth in it, the Q phenomenon being the clearest case. Both then point at the phrase needs must have been in Epiphanius on the date of Christ's birth, treating it as the same machinery that manufactures a savior figure every election cycle."}, {"title": "Witches as Knowers, Archons as Teachers", "body": "Kuhn's section on the three witches gets read in full: the witch is intrinsically masculine, derived from the Anglo-Saxon stem behind wit, wizard and the German wissen, and the broomstick is knowledge sweeping out the animal nature. Chance argues the witch was made a bogeyman precisely because she stands for gnosis, the way herbalism got tarred while it carried his family through pregnancy. Slick offers science as a socially acceptable seance. The closing note is that monsters and archons are tutelary spirits, a dojo rather than a prison, and that darkness deserves thanks."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Professional consciousness rippler and bass player extraordinaire, Jorge Mesa of Third Eye Edify joins us tonight for a chill hangout--we both had new children born a week ago, so we'll swap some cool stories about the births, dad-life, and who knows, maybe some Halloween/Samhain gravy too. It'll be a fun way for me to ease back into the live stream biz after taking a few weeks break.
